name: Araki
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: Word stress in Araki normally strikes the penultimate syllable, at least when the last syllable of the word is of the form -(C)V. A secondary stress may be heard on every second syllable towards the left of the word. ... As is clear in Table 2-15, stress is not assigned to a fixed syllable in the lexicon, but instead may change its position when a suffix is added. Another way to say this, is to consider that stress is assigned only after the lexeme has received all its affixes to form the whole phonological word. ... The simplest way is to say that words ending with a consonant, contrary to vowel-final words, normally receive their primary stress on their final syllable. [Table 2-19 Stress on the final syllable with words ending with C: malum [ma'lum] 'quiet', naru-m [na'rum] 'our child', hosu-n [ho'sun] 'this/here'] The last row of Table 2-19 stands for all the words which receive a -C…

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim in the open-access PDF we hold at the cited sections/pages (2.3.1 p.21; 2.3.3 p.23-24; 2.3.4 p.24). The deciding source is the standard and only reference grammar of this moribund language, written by its sole field linguist, with a six-page stress section; Glottolog has exactly one descriptive reference and the author's own bibliography shows no later phonological work. The classification (final stress if C-final, else penult; -VV# = two syllables; suffixes shift stress, clitics do not; alternating secondary stress leftward; listed lexical exceptions like cau, 1sg -á) matches François's explicit surface statement ('words ending with a consonant.. normally receive their primary stress on their final syllable', fn.27 Spanish comparison). One nuance worth keeping in mind but not requiring a reclassify: François derives the C-final pattern diachronically/derivationally from penul
